introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2025. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.

Question ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.

Each question that is sub-divided has the sub mark in brackets.

In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.

If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH paper are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.

NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

Calculators are Allowed.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) (i) Explain **THREE** proofs to show that the Earth is spherical in shape.
(ii) Distinguish between rotation of the earth and revolution of the earth.

(6+2=8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Three proofs that the Earth is spherical (6 marks, two marks each: the proof and its explanation).**

1. **Circumnavigation.** Travellers who sail or fly continuously in one direction, for example westwards, finally return to their starting point without turning back. The first voyage round the world was completed in 1519-1522 by the expedition that Magellan had begun. This is possible only on a body that is curved in every direction, like a sphere (a flat Earth would have an edge).
2. **Ships disappearing over the horizon.** A ship sailing away from the shore does not simply become smaller: its hull disappears first and the mast and funnel are seen last; a ship approaching shows the mast first and the hull afterwards. The hull is hidden by the curve of the sea surface, which shows that the surface is curved.
3. **The shadow of the Earth in an eclipse of the Moon.** During a lunar eclipse the shadow cast by the Earth on the Moon always has a **curved, circular edge**, whatever the position of the Earth. Only a sphere always casts a circular shadow.
4. **Photographs from space** (satellites and astronauts) show the Earth as a round globe.
5. **Other proofs that may be used:** the horizon is always circular and widens as the observer climbs higher; different places see the sun at different times (time zones), and observers see different stars as they move north or south (the Pole Star rises higher as one goes north).

(Any three, each clearly explained.)

**(ii) Rotation and revolution (2 marks, one mark each).**

| Rotation | Revolution |
|---|---|
| The spinning of the Earth on its own axis, from west to east | The movement of the Earth in its orbit (an elliptical path) round the Sun |
| One rotation takes about 24 hours (23 h 56 min exactly), and it causes day and night and the apparent daily movement of the sun | One revolution takes about 365 1/4 days (one year), and together with the tilt of the axis (23.5 degrees) it causes the seasons |
themes: evidence for the earth's spherical shape

questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Completed table (5 marks, one mark for each element).**

| Element | Instrument | Unit of measurement |
|---|---|---|
| Rainfall | Rain gauge | Millimetres (mm) |
| Hours of Sunshine | Sunshine recorder (the Campbell-Stokes sunshine recorder) | Hours (and tenths of an hour) per day |
| Temperature | Thermometer (a maximum and minimum thermometer, kept in a Stevenson screen) | Degrees Celsius (deg C) |
| Atmospheric pressure | Barometer (mercury or aneroid barometer) | Millibars (mb), or hectopascals (hPa) |
| Wind direction | Wind vane | Points of the compass (N, NE, E...) or degrees from north |

**(ii) Two precautions when setting a rain gauge (2 marks, one mark each).**

1. Put the gauge in an **open place, away from trees, buildings and fences**, so that they do not shelter the gauge or drip into it (the usual rule is a distance of at least twice the height of the obstacle).
2. Fix the gauge **firmly and upright, level, with the rim about 30 cm above the ground**, so that rain splashing from the ground does not enter the funnel and the gauge is not blown over.

(Other accepted precautions: put it on short grass or on gravel rather than on concrete; fence it against animals; read it at the same time every day.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) State:

- **TWO** inputs of the hydrological cycle,
- **THREE** benefits of waste management.

(2+3=5 marks)

Total (20 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Two inputs of the hydrological cycle (2 marks).**

1. **Precipitation** (rain, snow, hail, dew): the water that falls from the atmosphere onto the land and the sea.
2. **Solar energy** (heat from the sun): the source of energy that evaporates water and drives the whole cycle.

(For a river basin, the inflow of water from other areas, such as surface and underground flow from neighbouring basins, is also accepted as an input.)

**Three benefits of waste management (3 marks).**

1. **A cleaner, healthier environment:** collecting and disposing of waste properly reduces air, water and soil pollution and the spread of diseases (cholera, typhoid, malaria from mosquitoes breeding in rubbish).
2. **Saving of resources and money:** recycling and reuse (plastics, metals, paper, glass) saves raw materials and energy, and compost from organic waste improves the soil.
3. **Employment and income:** collection, sorting and recycling create jobs and earn money for households and councils; it also prevents the blocking of drains and so reduces floods in towns.
